study_identification.title: Closing the life-cycle of normative modeling using federated hierarchical Bayesian regression

study_characteristics.study_objective: This study aims to introduce a federated probabilistic framework using hierarchical Bayesian regression (HBR) to complete the life-cycle of normative modeling across massive multi-center neuroimaging datasets. The goal is to estimate a reference normative model across a massive population while addressing medical data privacy issues and dealing with nuisance variation such as variability in the image acquisition process.

dataset_name.answer: Multi-site aggregated dataset (ABCD; CamCAN; CMI; CNP; FCON; HCP; HCPAG; HCPDV; HCPEP; IXI; NKI; OASIS3; OPN; PNC; TOP; UKBB; 16 studies total)

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: FreeSurfer v5.3 and v6.0; Destrieux atlas for cortical parcellation (148 cortical regions); cortical thickness measures

quality_checking_detail.answer: Euler number threshold (median-centered absolute Euler number >25), excluded 1566 (4%) subjects due to low-quality images. Subjects were excluded if their scan-site median-centered absolute Euler number was higher than 25. The Euler numbers are computed as a part of standard recon-all FreeSurfer pipeline. Median centering is necessary because the Euler number is scaled differently for different datasets. The threshold of 25 was determined empirically by manually examining the excluded scans. Participants with missing demographic (age/sex) information were also excluded.

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: Hierarchical Bayesian regression (HBR) with scanner site as group-effect (hierarchical random effects) with site-specific homoscedastic variance. Sex also modeled as group-effect. The HBR provides partial pooling approach that estimates site-specific mean effects (fμ) and variations (f+σ) which are used to derive site-agnostic z-statistics. Compared to ComBat harmonization and fixed-effect pooling. HBR does not directly remove batch-related variability from data, thus preserves unknown sources of biological variations that correlate with batch-effects. The study demonstrates that HBR overcomes theoretical and practical limitations of ComBat harmonization including: 1) removing too much variance when site effects are correlated with effects of interest; 2) inability to preserve unknown biological variance (e.g., subtypes) correlated with site-effects; 3) practical issues in federated settings where access to all sites' data is required for parameter estimation.

predictor_effects.answer: Age: fixed effect; Sex: group-effect (hierarchical random effect); Scanner/Site: group-effect (hierarchical random effect) with site-specific homoscedastic variance. The HBR assumes θμ_i and θσ_i (parameters governing data generation for each batch) come exchangeably from the same prior distribution: θμ_i ~ N(μ_θμ, σ²_θμ) and θσ_i ~ N(μ_θσ, σ²_θσ). Weakly-informative Gaussian hyperpriors are used: μ_θμ, μ_θσ ~ N(0, 10³) and log(σ_θμ), log(σ_θσ) ~ N(0, 2.5).

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study explicitly addresses nuisance structure through multiple mechanisms: 1) Site-specific modeling of both mean and variance to handle additive and multiplicative batch effects; 2) Hierarchical Bayesian framework that models site-specific parameters while sharing information across sites; 3) Site-specific homoscedastic variance models to accommodate different noise levels across scanners; 4) Simulation studies (Fig S3 and S4) demonstrating HBR's ability to handle hidden site-specific factors affecting variability and slope; 5) Sex as group-effect to model sex-related differences; 6) Quality control using Euler numbers to handle measurement quality variation. The paper provides extensive theoretical discussion and empirical validation of how HBR handles various types of nuisance structure including mean shifts, variance differences, and correlations between covariates and site effects.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: In HBR, similar to no-pooling, we allow the model to learn different sets of parameters for data from multiple sites. At the same time, similar to complete pooling, the model has a fixed set of hyperparameters. Here, hyperparameters play the role of a joint prior over the parameters. They perform as a regularizer and prevent the model from overfitting on small batches... By using separate fμ and f+σ across batches, the z-statistics are respectively compensated for the additive and multiplicative batch-effects without the need to harmonize data primarily. Therefore, they accommodate batch-effects thorough modelling them explicitly in the generative model... In two exaggerated simulation scenarios, we assume that a hidden site-specific factor is present in the data... the HBR provides a reasonably good estimate of quantiles for two sites.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.location: Main text pages discussing HBR methodology (lines 154-173 in materials/Kia2022.pdf.md); Simulation study in S1 File (lines 34-69 in materials/Kia2022_sup.pdf.md); Fig 2 (line 126); Results section demonstrating site-effect removal (lines 292-293, 302-304)

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study validates the normative model using 20% held-out test data from the same training datasets in the multi-site data regression experiment. This represents same-domain non-independent validation where data are split within each site/scanner. The validation is performed 10 times with different random train-test splits. Three validation metrics are used: Pearson's correlation coefficient (RHO), standardized mean squared error (SMSE), and mean standardized log-loss (MSLL). The MSLL metric specifically evaluates both central tendency and variance fit. Additionally, site-effect removal is validated using SVM classification of z-scores across datasets.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: In the multi-site data regression setting, the goal is to compare the performance of HBR with naive pooling, fixed-effect pooling, pooling after data harmonization, and no-pooling models in deriving the normative range of cortical thicknesses across 148 brain areas. Here, we assume the data from all scanners are available when estimating the normative model, i.e., a centralized data architecture. In each experimental run, 80% of healthy samples are randomly selected to train the regression model. The remaining 20% are used for the evaluation... All experiments and evaluations are repeated ten times with different random healthy participants in the training and test phases. Three metrics are used to evaluate the quality of fits, i) Pearson's correlation coefficient (RHO) between observed and predicted brain measures; ii) standardized mean squared error (SMSE), and iii) mean standardized log-loss (MSLL).
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.location: Materials and methods - Experiments section (lines 256-261 in materials/Kia2022.pdf.md)

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: While the model adaptation experiment uses clinical datasets (CNP, HCPEP, OASIS3, TOP) that were not used in the reference model training (trained on ABCD, CAMCAN, CMI, FCON, HCP, HCPAG, HCPDV, IXI, NKI, OPN, PNC, UKBB), this represents model deployment/transfer learning rather than pure independent validation of the original model. The study shows performance on these datasets after model adaptation, but does not clearly describe a traditional independent validation where the reference model trained on one set of sites is tested on completely held-out sites without adaptation. The model extension experiment compares centralized vs. decentralized training but uses synthetic data generation rather than true held-out sites.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: In the model adaptation setting, we demonstrate an application of HBR in a more realistic clinical scenario when the aim is to adapt the parameters of a reference normative model to private clinical data at local hospitals. To do so, we first use a linear homoscedastic model to estimate the parameters of the reference normative model on datasets with only healthy participants (ABCD, CAMCAN, CMI, FCON, HCP, HCPAG, HCPDV, IXI, NKI OPN, PNC, and UKBB). Then, in each run 50% of random healthy participants in clinical datasets, including CNP, HCPEP, OASIS3, and TOP are used to recalibrate the parameters of the reference model. The rest of the healthy participants and patients are used as test samples.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.location: Materials and methods - Experiments section (lines 263-265 in materials/Kia2022.pdf.md); Model adaptation results (Fig 10, lines 298-300)

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The study includes clinical populations (patients with ADHD, SZ, BD, MDD, EP, MCI, DM) which represent a different domain (pathological vs. normative) from the healthy control training data. The anomaly detection experiment evaluates whether patient deviations from normative ranges show clinically meaningful patterns. However, this is not traditional cross-domain validation but rather clinical application of normative models. The regional AUC analysis shows significant and stable results for dementia (AUC 0.64-0.68), schizophrenia (AUC 0.58-0.61), and early psychosis (AUC 0.59), demonstrating the model can detect meaningful deviations in different clinical populations. The study acknowledges this is unsupervised anomaly detection rather than supervised classification.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: In the anomaly detection experiment, we aim to exemplify a possible application of the full cycle of normative modeling (i.e., developing a reference normative model on a large healthy population and model adaptation to clinical data) in data-driven biomarker discovery... The abnormal probability indices for each individual across 148 cortical regions are computed. Then, the region-wise areas under the ROC curves (AUCs) are derived to evaluate the predictive power of deviations for each diagnostic label... Only significant and stable areas that pass the FDR correction in 9 or more out of 10 full experimental runs are reported... In dementia cases, the best performances are observed in the occipital and temporal lobes including bilateral occipitotemporal (fusiform) gyrus (AUC = 0.68 and 0.64)... In patients with schizophrenia, our results show the concentration of distinctive areas in the frontal lobe including the right orbital inferior frontal gyrus (AUC = 0.61)... Even though these performances are lower than the state-of-the-art in classifying dementia and schizophrenia patients from healthy participants, it is important to consider the fact that our anomaly detection method is, in contrast, an unsupervised approach.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.location: Materials and methods - Experiments section (lines 266-267 in materials/Kia2022.pdf.md); Results - The deviations are distinctive (lines 308-351); Fig 11-13 showing clinical validation

deviation_metric.answer: Z-score (Eq 1: z = (y - fμ(X,θμ)) / f+σ(X,θσ)); Abnormal Probability Index (Pabn) computed from z-scores using area in tails of normal distribution: Pabn(z) = 2(1 - Φ(|z|)) where Φ is cumulative distribution function of normal distribution. Pabn ranges from 0 (no deviation) to 1 (extreme deviation). Used for unsupervised anomaly detection.

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Region-wise Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) to evaluate the predictive power of deviations (abnormal probability indices) for each diagnosis across 148 cortical regions. Statistical significance assessed using permutation tests with 1000 repetitions and false discovery rate (FDR) correction for multiple comparisons. Only significant and stable AUCs (passing FDR correction in 9 or more out of 10 experimental runs) were reported. Case-control discrimination using abnormal probability indices as predictors. Visualization of patient deviations relative to normative ranges stratified by sex. SVM classification (C=1, 5-fold stratified cross-validation) used to evaluate site-effect removal in z-statistics by attempting to classify datasets in one-vs-one scenario; balanced accuracies near chance level (0.53) for HBR, ComBat, and fixed-effect methods confirm site-effect removal (vs. 0.90 for naive pooling).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: HBR successfully derives accurate normative ranges handling site-effects without data harmonization, enables federated learning on decentralized data, and detects clinically meaningful deviations in dementia (occipital/temporal lobes, AUC 0.64-0.68), schizophrenia (frontal lobe, AUC 0.58-0.61), and early psychosis (temporal regions, AUC 0.59) using unsupervised anomaly detection.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: The study demonstrates that hierarchical Bayesian regression (HBR) provides superior performance for multi-site normative modeling compared to naive pooling, fixed-effect pooling, pooling after ComBat harmonization, and no-pooling approaches. HBR shows equivalently better regression performance to fixed-effect modeling (evaluated by RHO, SMSE, MSLL across 148 cortical regions) while offering advantages for federated learning. The extended HBR model trained on decentralized data shows very close performance to centralized training (R²=0.98 for RHO, 0.97 for SMSE, 0.95 for MSLL), confirming feasibility of model estimation on distributed data without data sharing. Model adaptation experiments demonstrate that transferring knowledge from reference models trained on large datasets (ABCD, CamCAN, CMI, FCON, HCP, HCPAG, HCPDV, IXI, NKI, OPN, PNC, UKBB) to clinical datasets improves performance over no-pooling approaches trained only on local data. Few-shot learning capability is demonstrated with reasonable normative ranges estimated even on tiny datasets (0-1 training samples per site/sex group) through informative priors. Clinical validation shows significant and stable deviations: In dementia (n=271), best discrimination in occipital and temporal regions including bilateral occipitotemporal/fusiform gyrus (AUC=0.68, 0.64), right middle temporal gyrus (AUC=0.65), and right superior/transverse occipital sulcus (AUC=0.65). In schizophrenia (n=265), distinctive deviations in frontal regions including right orbital inferior frontal gyrus (AUC=0.61), right medial orbital sulcus (AUC=0.60), and left superior frontal gyrus (AUC=0.58). In early psychosis (n=123), only right middle temporal gyrus showed significant stable results (AUC=0.59). Site-effect removal evaluation shows balanced classification accuracy drops from 0.90 (naive pooling) to ~0.53 (HBR, ComBat, fixed-effect), confirming effective site-effect mitigation. The total dataset included 37,126 scans from 79 scanners covering ages 6-100 years after quality control excluded 1,566 (4%) low-quality scans based on Euler number threshold >25.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: 1) Current implementation assumes Gaussian likelihood, which may not be well-calibrated for skewed or bounded phenotype distributions, though extensions to non-Gaussian models are mentioned as ongoing work; 2) Models are estimated separately for each brain region without accounting for inter-regional correlations, meaning only univariate site-effects are removed and some multivariate site-effects may remain (evidenced by above-chance classification in Fig 8); 3) While Euler number-based quality control was used, fully automated quality control methods for massive datasets remain an open challenge; 4) Linear models were primarily used; while sufficient for cortical thickness, other measures may require non-linear or heteroscedastic models; 5) Dementia patients from OASIS3 were only mild cases, limiting comparability with studies using more advanced dementia; 6) Clinical AUC performance (0.58-0.68) is lower than supervised classification approaches, though this is expected for unsupervised anomaly detection; 7) Some disorders (ADHD, BD, MDD, MCI) did not show significant and stable deviations passing the rigorous stability criteria (significant in 9/10 runs); 8) Model extension using synthetic data generation may have slightly lower MSLL performance compared to centralized training in some regions.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: This study presents a complete federated learning life-cycle for normative modeling addressing real-world clinical deployment challenges including data privacy, multi-site harmonization, model updating, and adaptation to small local datasets. Key innovations include: 1) Federated probabilistic framework enabling model estimation without data sharing; 2) Model extension mechanism allowing incremental updates as new datasets become available; 3) Model adaptation via parameter transfer learning enabling few-shot learning on small clinical datasets; 4) Preservation of unknown biological variance correlated with site-effects (unlike ComBat); 5) Flexible framework accommodating different parametric/non-parametric, linear/non-linear, homoscedastic/heteroscedastic modeling choices. The paper emphasizes HBR is not a harmonization method per se - site-related variance remains in predictions (fμ) while z-statistics are site-agnostic. The approach is similar to both meta-analysis (second-level parameters estimated per site) and mega-analysis (first-level hyperparameters estimated jointly). Clinical relevance is demonstrated through precision psychiatry applications where individual deviation patterns can be mapped, addressing heterogeneity in complex brain disorders. Future directions include: extending to non-Gaussian likelihoods using GAMLSS framework; modeling multivariate inter-regional correlations using Wishart priors; developing robust automated quality control; exploring likelihood warping for arbitrary distributions; and applying to multi-center consortia like ENIGMA.

general_notes.general_notes: This is a methodologically rigorous paper introducing federated hierarchical Bayesian regression for normative modeling. Full list of 16 datasets: ABCD (n=10,732, 29 scanners, age 9-11), CamCAN (n=647, 1 scanner, age 18-88), CMI (n=893, 2 scanners, age 18-88), CNP (n=264 with 139 patients, 2 scanners, age 21-50), FCON (n=1,021 with 25 ADHD, 18 scanners, age 8-85), HCP Young Adult (n=1,113, 1 scanner, age 22-37), HCPAG (n=677, 5 scanners, age 36-100), HCPDV (n=653, 5 scanners, age 8-22), HCPEP (n=180 with 123 EP, 4 scanners, age 17-36), IXI (n=557, 1 scanner, age 20-86), NKI (n=482, 1 scanner, age 6-85), OASIS3 (n=2,044 with 322 patients, 5 scanners, age 43-97), OpenNeuro (n=612, 6 scanners, age 8-58), PNC (n=1,514, 1 scanner, age 8-23), TOP (n=823 with 498 patients, 1 scanner, age 17-69), UK Biobank (n=14,914, 2 scanners, age 44-80). Total: 37,126 scans from 79 scanners after QC, 36,019 healthy controls, 1,107 patients. FreeSurfer versions mixed (5.3: HCP, OASIS3; 6.0: all others). Python implementation available in PCNtoolkit v0.18 at https://github.com/amarquand/PCNtoolkit using PyMC3 for inference with No-U-Turn sampler (NUTS). ComBat harmonization implementation from https://github.com/Warvito/neurocombat_sklearn. The paper includes extensive supplementary materials with theoretical analysis of ComBat limitations (Fig S1), simulation studies demonstrating HBR advantages (Fig S3-S4), and comparison of homoscedastic vs. heteroscedastic models (Fig S5). Study received funding from NWO VIDI fellowships, ERC consolidator grant, Wellcome Trust awards, and Marie Sklodowska-Curie grant. Competing interests noted: Ole A. Andreassen is consultant to HealthLytix and received speaker's honorarium from Lundbeck; Christian F. Beckmann is shareholder and director of SBG Neuro. TOP dataset subject to clinical data privacy restrictions. The study emphasizes model portability and real-world applicability over theoretical performance, prioritizing federated learning capabilities and few-shot adaptation over maximum prediction accuracy.
